description: Device testing, signing, beta testing, store listings, and releases.

screens.body:
Emulators are great for fast iteration, but they lie a little. They don't feel like a real phone: performance is different, sensors are faked, gestures feel wrong, and that weird crash only happens on one manufacturer's skin.

Before any release, test on real devices — ideally a cheap old phone and a new one. Your users don't all own flagships.

options: Real devices — emulators fake sensors and performance
check.question: Before release, test on…

screens.heading: Emulators lie a little
screens.keyPoint: Real devices catch what emulators can't.

screens.body:
Stores need proof an app really came from you. That's code signing: a cryptographic certificate stamps your app bundle, and the phone verifies the stamp before installing.

iOS uses provisioning profiles and certificates from Apple; Android uses a keystore file you must guard with your life. Lose your Android signing key and you can never update your app again — same app, new key, store says no.

options: It proves the app really came from you
check.question: Code signing exists because…

screens.heading: Signing your app
screens.keyPoint: Your signing key is your identity — never lose it.

screens.body:
Beta testing puts your app in real users' hands before the public launch. iOS has TestFlight; Android has internal, closed, and open testing tracks. Friends, classmates, and friendly users find the crashes your emulator never will.

Ship betas early and often. A crash found by a tester is embarrassing; a crash found by ten thousand users is a one-star avalanche.

options: TestFlight on iOS, testing tracks on Android
check.question: Beta testing happens through…

screens.heading: Beta testing
screens.keyPoint: Real testers find real crashes before launch.

screens.body:
Your store listing is a marketing page: icon, app name, screenshots, a short description, and keywords. Most users decide in seconds, from screenshots alone.

Show the app doing its best thing in the first two screenshots. Write the description for humans first, search second. And localize the listing if you want users beyond your own country.

options: Screenshots showing the app's best moments
check.question: What sells an app in the store?

screens.heading: The store listing
screens.keyPoint: Your listing is marketing — screenshots decide in seconds.

screens.body:
Both Apple and Google review every app before it goes live. Reviews take hours to days, and rejections are normal: crashes on launch, broken links, placeholder text, missing privacy disclosures.

Read the review guidelines before you submit, not after your first rejection. Fix, resubmit, and keep a checklist of past rejections so you never repeat one.

options: Crashes, broken links, missing privacy info
check.question: Common rejection reasons include…

screens.heading: Review and rejection
screens.keyPoint: Read the guidelines first; rejections are normal.

screens.body:
A staged rollout releases to a small slice of users first — 1%, then 10%, then everyone — while you watch crash reports. If something's broken, you halt the rollout instead of burning your whole user base.

Both stores support this. Never ship a big rewrite to 100% on day one unless you enjoy emergency patches at midnight.

options: Release to a small % first, watch crashes, then expand
check.question: A staged rollout means…

screens.heading: Rollouts
screens.keyPoint: Ramp up gradually; halt fast if crashes spike.

screens.body:
Users update at wildly different speeds — some on day one, some six months later. Version numbers (1.4.0) tell users what's new; build numbers tell you exactly which binary crashed.

Keep your API backward-compatible with older app versions, or force-update when you truly must. And never assume everyone runs your latest code.
screens.heading: Versioning and updates
screens.keyPoint: Support old versions — users update on their own schedule.
